catalog_quote: [p.67, sec. 3.2 声調] 音節声調を持ち、開音節において、高平調 (High-level)、中平調 (Mid-level)、低下降調 (Low-falling)、高下降調 (High-falling) の 4 つの声調を持つ。ただし、閉鎖音末子音を持つ閉音節においては、High と Low の 2 声調のみが対立する。 [pp.68-69, sec. 3.4.2.1 副音節] 二音節語の大部分 (基礎語彙中約 74%) は副音節をその第一音節に持つ。ジンポー語の副音節の特徴は次のように一般化することができる。副音節は 1) 母音が /ə/ である、2) 声調を持たない、3) 強勢を持たない、4) 開音節である (cf. *kən, *pət) 、5) 単語末には現れない (cf. *kə#, *ɡumpə#)、6) 子音結合を持たない (cf. *krə, *pyə)。 [p.72, sec. 3.4.3] この種の成節鼻音は丁寧に発音された場合、声調を持つように発音されることがあるが、しばしば非強勢で発音されその場合は声調が曖昧になる。成節鼻音のピッチが語の弁別に用いられることはないため、本稿では、音韻的には成節鼻音は声調を持たないものと考える。成節鼻音は 1) 二音節語の第一音節にのみ出現する 2) 単語末には現れない 3) しばしば非強勢で発音される 4) 声調を持たない、などの点で先述の副音節と類似性を見せる。 [Kurabe 2017:16] The vast majority of disyllabic words take the form of the iambic (right-dominant) structure, consisting of a heavy syllable preceded by a light syllable that has a phonetically short schwa or syllabic nasal as its nucleus.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [p.68] 二音節語の大部分 (基礎語彙中約 74%) は副音節をその第一音節に持つ。ジンポー語の副音節の特徴は次のように一般化することができる。副音節は 1) 母音が /ə/ である、2) 声調を持たない、3) 強勢を持たない、4) 開音節である (cf. *kən, *pət) 、5) 単語末には現れない (cf. *kə#, *ɡumpə#)、6) 子音結合を持たない (cf. *krə, *pyə)。 [p.72] 成節鼻音は 1) 二音節語の第一音節にのみ出現する 2) 単語末には現れない 3) しばしば非強勢で発音される 4) 声調を持たない、などの点で先述の副音節と類似性を見せる。
new_statements.translation: [p.68] The majority of disyllabic words (about 74% of the basic vocabulary) have a minor syllable as their first syllable. The properties of the Jinghpaw minor syllable can be generalised as follows: a minor syllable 1) has the vowel /ə/, 2) has no tone, 3) has no stress, 4) is an open syllable (cf. *kən, *pət), 5) does not occur word-finally (cf. *kə#, *gumpə#), 6) has no consonant cluster (cf. *krə, *pyə). [p.72] Syllabic nasals resemble the minor syllables just described in that they 1) occur only as the first syllable of disyllabic words, 2) do not occur word-finally, 3) are often pronounced unstressed, 4) carry no tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jinghpaw is a syllable-tone language (4 tones on smooth syllables, 2 on checked). Native words are mono- or disyllabic; most disyllables are sesquisyllabic (Cə- or N̩- presyllable + full syllable) and the presyllable is toneless and unstressed, so prominence sits on the final, full (tone-bearing) syllable: an iambic / right-dominant word pattern, which Kurabe states in English elsewhere ('iambic (right-dominant) structure', Onsei Kenkyu 21(3):16, 2017; 'iambic prosodic pattern', Gengo Kenkyu 153, 2018; AALL 15:48, 2021). No stress rule is given for the minority of full CVC+CVC disyllables (gùmrà 'horse' type) or for compounds; the colonial grammars disagree there (Hanson 1896 p.19: accent on the first syllable of 'pure dissyllabic words', Gum'ra; Hertz 1902 p.3: accent 'as a rule rests on the last syllable in dissyllabic words', exceptions chiefly noun+noun compounds).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Kurabe. Hertz 1902 p.3: in trisyllables the accent is on the last syllable 'with a slight accent on the first'.
new_statements.exceptions: Kurabe 2012: none for the minor-syllable rule; sesquisyllabization variants (gìnsúp ~ gəsúp) in fast speech. Kurabe 2017 fn.2: the northern-Burma dialect is losing tonal contrasts on schwa light syllables. Hertz 1902: compound nouns (shan'hpi, wan'li, lup'wa), some adverbs and reduplicated adjectives, and words in -sha (penult accent) are exceptions to final accent. Hanson 1896: accent shifts onto particles when two or more follow, onto the auxiliary in verb+auxiliary, and onto negative n-.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (monomorphemic word structure, citation forms) in Kurabe; Hanson 1896's accent rules extend over word + case/tense particles, i.e. partly phrase-level, and neither Hanson nor Hertz writes tone, so their 'accent' may conflate tone and stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kurabe 2012 describes Standard Jinghpaw as spoken in Myitkyina, Kachin State, Myanmar (fieldwork 2009-2011) = the Myanmar standard (Manmaw/Bhamo-Myitkyina) variety, i.e. Glottolog Southern Jinghpaw kach1280; Hanson 1896 and Hertz 1902 describe the same Bhamo-area 'Kachin/Chingpaw'. Kurabe 2017 (Onsei Kenkyu) draws its data from the dialect spoken in China (Xu et al. 1983, Dai & Xu 1992, Dai 2012 = Nkhum/Enkun), which Kurabe 2014 groups with Standard Jingpho in the Southern branch; his fn.2 notes the northern-Burma dialect is losing tonal contrasts on schwa light syllables. All distinct from sing1264 Singpho/Turung (Northern Jinghpaw), which is already in the catalog.

sources.note: Sec. 7 'Accentuation' pp.19-20: with preformatives ga-, ka-, la- etc. 'the accent always rests on the ultima', also when particles follow; 'In pure dissyllabic words the accent rests on the first syllable. Gum'ra; num'sha', shifting to the ultima when two particles follow; verbs keep accent on root ultima; negative n- attracts 'the stress of the voice'. Tones (5) described separately but not.
